hook.text: The Penrose triangle looks like a solid 3D object on paper—until you trace its edges and find they can't connect.

buildup.text: Impossible figures exploit local consistency: each corner looks correct, but the global structure contradicts itself.

discovery.text: Your brain processes depth cues locally, not globally. It accepts each junction before noticing the whole is impossible.

twist.text: M.C. Escher built entire worlds from these contradictions—staircases that climb forever, water that flows uphill.

climax.text: Impossible figures reveal that 3D perception is assembled from local rules, not a unified spatial model.

punchline.text: Your brain builds depth one corner at a time.

quiz.question: Why do impossible figures look plausible at first?
options: The brain processes depth cues locally
